This study develops a novel time-varying count model called the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) to analyze data with nonlinear patterns, abrupt changes, and zero-inflated patterns. The TV-PARX model differentiates itself from existing time-varying count models by employing a local linear regression technique to update parameter estimates when structural breaks occur. Additionally, we propose an efficient Bayesian Inference scheme to analyze TV-PARX models. Compared to existing methods, our local linear regression approach significantly reduces computational costs associated with high-breakpoint densities. To assess the accuracy of our variable selection approach, we introduce a local linearized posterior distribution. Empirical analyses on real-world data sets and a simulation study demonstrate that the TV-PARX model delivers superior performance compared to existing time-varying count models.

Vertical aerosol optical depth (τa) can be accurately determined using a method that combines wide-field photometry and a model of the aerosol-free angular dependence of stellar light. This approach doesn't rely on absolutely calibrated photometry, unlike traditional methods. By taking advantage of both wide-field photometry and spectroscopy, and assuming a fixed aerosol model, a precise determination of τa is possible. Based on this calculation, a correction can be applied to remove aerosol effects when identifying supernovae. A test of this method using real data from the ATLAS all-sky camera system and the TELESCOPE INFRARED SUPPORT SYSTEM (TIRSS) on the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency's (JAXA) GOSAT satellite showed its effectiveness. As a result, multiple supernovae were discovered within a few hours of explosion, precluding the need for follow-up observations with telescopes. One supernova was discovered 10 hours before it could be observed with a conventional telescope.

Numerous numerical approaches have been developed to solve the Ab initio electron-nucleus interaction in quantum chemistry, with some methods suited for real-time evolution and others for post-determination. A new numerical scheme, dubbed the Discrete Adaptive Multilevel (DAM) approach, has been introduced and compared with existing methods such as the trapezoidal rule, Filon's formula, and the recursive exponential formula on alanine dipeptide models. Utilizing the DAM approach within a Hartree-Fock framework led to notable improvements in accuracy with a minor increase in computational complexity. When combining the DAM method with an existing post-determination scheme, recursive exponential formula, notable enhancements in accuracy were observed with minimal loss in efficiency. These findings suggest the DAM approach offers a promising alternative for real-time Ab initio calculations.

Artificial intelligence has greatly improved image classification for the visually impaired.
However, a significant gap remains in effectively describing images for classification.
To address this shortcoming, our project develops an interactive system that generates detailed descriptions
of images through a collaborative process between visually impaired individuals and AI technology.
This system leverages a Generative Pre-trained Transformer 3 as the image classification model.
We also created instructional materials to assist users in describing images accurately.
To ensure high-quality descriptions, we established strict guidelines that users must follow.
An empirical study with six visually impaired participants revealed that our system significantly enhances
image classification accuracy compared to users providing descriptions independently.
All participants demonstrated a strong desire to use our system in real-world situations.

We provide a novel approach to solving optimization problems in quantum field theory by deriving certain Euler-Arnold equations through a variational perspective. Initially, we define appropriate abstract frameworks for Euler-Arnold equations and outline the necessary conditions for an equation to be considered an Euler-Arnold equation. Subsequently, we derive specific Euler-Arnold equation structures that are relevant to optimization problems in quantum field theory. Moreover, we establish a direct connection between these derived Euler-Arnold equations and the underlying optimization problems by demonstrating that an equation corresponds to an optimization problem when an integrand condition is met. This condition is further analyzed, and an alternative representation is obtained for certain Euler-Arnold equations through a regularity argument. Finally, we outline the steps necessary to apply the derived Euler-Arnold equation frameworks to specific quantum field theory optimization problems.

The interaction dynamics of heavy quarks are crucial for understanding various processes in QCD. A key process of interest is the formation of heavy quark-antiquark bound states, specifically charmonium and bottomonium. While 2-loop calculations provide accurate predictions for contributing processes, the overall interaction is most effectively described by combining these processes and employing an effective theory like NRQCD. Recently, the glueball spectrum has been calculated using a similar approach, indicating that 2-loop contributions are necessary for predicting certain process outcomes. Building upon this success, we have extended our previous work on heavy quark-antiquark bound states to calculate 2-loop corrections for the process $g\gamma\to\bar{Q}Q$ and its contributing diagrams. We have also determined the applicable energy range for the process by analyzing the bound state formation process itself. Furthermore, we have calculated the 2-loop correction to the process $g\gamma\to\bar{Q}Q$ within the FSR approximation, which allows for the inclusion of both real and virtual photon processes. We have also determined the applicable energy range for the process by analyzing the bound state formation process itself. The calculation employs an effective theory similar to NRQCD, specifically the heavy quark effective theory (HQET), which is suitable for describing the low-momentum dynamics of heavy quarks. This research develops wideband waveforming techniques that adapt to fair-throughput and total-throughput optimization problems. Initially, we establish a performance benchmark by resolving the fair-throughput problem using a dynamic programming approach with a time complexity of $O(n^3)$, where $n$ represents the number of users. Subsequently, we devise an iterative algorithm to solve the total-throughput problem with a time complexity of $O(n^3)$ by leveraging the fair-throughput solution. Moreover, we develop a simpler algorithm to solve the total-throughput problem with a time complexity of $O(nk)$, where $k$ denotes the codebook size.

To fit PDFs at various scales, researchers employ an evolution formula called DGLAP, which is based on an integral that doesn't have a straightforward closed-form solution, necessitating the use of numerical tools like FitPak. A new approach to fitting PDFs at different scales has been developed, utilizing a discrete evolution method (NADA) that solves DGLAP equations directly, eliminating the need for numerical tools. By employing NADA, fits can be performed at specific scales without recalculating previously determined fits, reducing the overall fitting process to a more manageable level. A demonstration of this method's effectiveness has been achieved by fitting NNPDF40_lucien data using NADA, with minor differences observed compared to the FitPak results. A C++ implementation of NADA has been made available on GitHub.

This research seeks to identify an optimal combustion model that fits within a linearized framework for analyzing turbulent, reacting flows. The framework in question focuses on small perturbations around an equilibrium state and utilizes the linearized form of the reaction rate term in the combustion model. A comprehensive analysis was conducted across various combustion models, including the Lagrangian and Eulerian approaches, as well as detailed and simplified Chemical Mechanism models. The analysis aimed to determine conditions under which the linearized reaction rate would meet specific criteria. The results revealed that the simplest CM model, supplemented by a library of pre-computed reactions, provided the best outcomes. This model consisted of an equilibrium air mixture at 25°C and 1 atmosphere, which reacted with a methane gas at varying temperatures and pressures. The most suitable conditions occurred when a methane gas was mixed with an equilibrium air mixture at 25°C and 1 atmosphere. The analysis also found that the simplest CM model met the desired conditions, which served as a baseline for further analysis.

This study introduces a novel constitutive relation within the framework of nonlocal gravity, differing from the standard relation used in the effective field theory approach. Our new relation is specifically tied to observable quantities, involving the energy-momentum tensor and a nonlocal operator. The purpose of this new relation is to account for the remaining terms in the Einstein-Hilbert action that are not covered by the standard relation. The new relation is shown to be equivalent to an additional constant times the Einstein curvature tensor, integrated over a specific region of the energy-momentum tensor. The parameter in the nonlocal relation is found to be directly linked with the same constant, indicating that both the relation and the tensor share similar characteristics. The new relation is found to be relevant for describing phenomena involving strong gravitational fields and massive objects, such as black holes and neutron stars, within the context of general relativity. It is also relevant for describing weak field limit effects, similar to the Einstein curvature tensor. The new relation is shown to be an essential component in modifying the Poisson equation in the nonlocal gravity model, in a similar manner to how the standard relation does so in the standard effective field theory approach.

A multidimensional analysis of $K^{\rm S}$0 identification in p+p collisions at 200 GeV is presented, utilizing 5.4 nb^-1 of $\sqrt{s}$ = 200 GeV p+p data collected by the STAR experiment at RHIC. Through the decay $K^{\rm S}$0$\rightarrow\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$, transverse momentum spectra and inflation rates of strange quarks and jets are compared and contrasted. While open charm and beauty jets have shorter lifetimes and decay into muons before reaching the detector, their spectra can be inferred from established benchmarks. Utilizing a Monte Carlo model, the composition of $K^{\rm S}$0 and its connection to jet fragmentation are examined. Based on this analysis, possible patterns of $K^{\rm S}$0, open charm, and beauty transverse momentum spectra in p+p collisions at 200 GeV and 2.76 TeV are predicted.

The connection between neutron star low mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) and millisecond pulsars in the galaxy remains unclear due to limited data. A recent study enhancing the sample of known LMXBs and searching for unknown pulsars in the galaxy's center could help bridge this gap. By applying new constraints based on binary evolution theory, researchers found that nearly all near-by LMXBs contain a neutron star, with a few exceptions likely containing a black hole. This high prevalence of LMXBs likely contributed to the formation of many millisecond pulsars in the galaxy. In fact, enough binary systems with a neutron star should have existed at some point that nearly all visible millisecond pulsars today originated from an LMXB. This discovery supports the idea that many millisecond pulsars are born in binary systems and suggests that the majority of near-by millisecond pulsars probably have an unseen companion star.

A bipartite graph is considered fully embedded when its edge set can be drawn as non-intersecting areas within a plane. We present an enhancement to the standard technique of vertex splitting that can be used to guarantee an embedding of a bipartite graph $G$. This enhancement results in a new set of bipartite subgraphs derived from the original graph. Previously, it was proven that vertex splitting could ensure an embedding for graphs with maximum degree three. Building on this, our approach leads to an $O(2^k \cdot n)$ time complexity for drawing graphs with a vertex splitting distance of $k$ between two given subgraphs with $n$ vertices. We also established an upper bound of $O(2^k \cdot \binom{n}{2})$ time complexity for drawing an entire graph with a vertex splitting distance of $k$ between two given subgraphs with $n$ vertices.

This research develops a novel technique, HyperDegrade, designed to enhance the effectiveness of Flush+Reload side-channel attacks when employing time-grained measurement systems that are prone to inaccuracy. HyperDegrade involves an optimized degradation process to pinpoint memory event occurrences, which can be challenged by the imprecision of these systems. To utilize this technique, we have developed two new attack vectors: an enhanced Flush+Reload attack and an TPA-based Flush+Reload attack. HyperDegrade significantly improves the efficacy of these attacks by significantly reducing the number of required memory access traces and enhancing time granularity. Our findings demonstrate that our hyperparameter-optimal HyperDegrade variant achieves the best results, taking just 10 microseconds to detect events and requiring fewer than 1000 traces in the worst-case scenario. We have also conducted real-world experiments on various Linux systems to validate our hyperparameter selection methodology, which are available on our project website.

This study delves into the world of knot theory and makes significant contributions to our understanding of a specific knot type known as the $(4n+1)$-crossed rail knot, as well as the $n$-shovel knot. A knot is considered "rail-like" if its diagram consists entirely of straight segments connected at right angles, with no repeated segments except at the ends. Our findings reveal that all rail-like knots can be rearranged through a series of simple, localized alterations called "diagonal moves," in addition to the established "swapping moves." What's more, we identify patterns that allow for the creation of new rail-like knots by combining existing ones, and we outline a step-by-step process to generate all possible rail-like knots with 10 or fewer segments.

We investigate how knowledge of task difficulty distributions influences the optimal policies for agents in a multi-agent system, tasked with completing various jobs on available machines. It is established that both agents and managers benefit from sharing information about task complexity, as it enables more efficient organization and reduces search time for both parties. To efficiently utilize this information, a new framework is proposed that combines the policy search with the learning process for the agent and a linear programming-based evaluation process for the manager. This framework results in higher average payoff compared to an existing model that assumes an unknown task difficulty distribution. Furthermore, to facilitate practical applications, it is shown that certain patterns of task difficulty distributions meet the model's requirements. One such example involves a scenario with multiple tasks of varying priorities, where higher payoffs are associated with more desirable outcomes.

We provide a comprehensive explanation for a category of regular groups whose actions align with a specific structure called Cartesian Decomposition, in addition to defining a new concept called Coherent Depth which serves as a measure of this structure. Within this framework, we establish a direct connection between groups with regular actions and those with diagonal subgroups that are closed under taking normal closures. Furthermore, we present an algorithm to determine the coherent depth of a given group through a series of recursive applications of the Godement's criterion, in combination with standard computational tools for identifying subgroups that are closed under normal closure.

Building upon the conventional Michelson optical interferometer design, we have developed and analyzed a novel optical interferometer structure called the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer. By introducing an additional 90-degree rotated mirror and adjusting the optical path differences between Sagnac and Michelson interferometer configurations, our sloshing-Sagnac design enables the simultaneous measurement of strain and angular deformations. Utilizing a quantum noise analysis, we have found that the sloshing-Sagnac design offers enhanced sensitivity for gravitational-wave detection compared to traditional Michelson and Sagnac interferometer designs. Specifically, we have discovered that the sloshing-Sagnac design outperforms Sagnac design sensitivity by an order of magnitude for low-frequency gravitational waves and has better high-frequency noise performance for strain sensors.

To enhance random access (RA) performance in extremely large multi-user multi-input multi-output (XL-MIMO) systems, our proposed novel protocol, NOVR-XL RA, extends the conventional single-user protocol to include an additional large-complexity list. By employing a threshold-based approach to dimension list size, our method achieves significant gains over existing strategies. Specifically, we derived closed-form expressions for the average number of successful transmissions and the throughput of NOVR-XL RA in terms of signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR). Furthermore, we demonstrated the practical applicability of our findings by calculating the average number of successful transmissions and throughput through numerical evaluations. Compared to existing protocols, our NOVR-XL RA exhibits substantial improvements in both throughput and the number of successful transmissions even at moderate system configurations.

Neural language models have been highly effective in tasks like machine translation and text summarization, often surpassing $N$-gram models. However, a key limitation of these neural models is their computational expense, making them difficult to use in real-time applications. In contrast, $N$-gram models are fast and efficient but generally deliver lower performance. We present a novel approach that bridges the gap between these models by leveraging the statistical patterns in $N$-gram models and incorporating them into the structure of neural language models. Our method allows for easily adjusting the model's balance between statistical and learned components. Through extensive experiments on large datasets from Google, IWSLT, and DUC, we demonstrate that our combination approach consistently yields improved performance over individual neural and $N$-gram models. Notably, our findings indicate that the best results are achieved when the $N$-gram model matches the neural model's context size. Our code is available on GitHub.

This research seeks to enhance the accuracy of vote tabulation through the integration of a spell correction component into an OCR system, targeting the local context. Initially, a training dataset is compiled to create a spell correction model utilizing the Levenshtein distance. Then, to evaluate the algorithm's effectiveness, various spell correction protocols are designed. Notably, the research finds that the spell correction algorithm contributes significantly to the accuracy of OCR output in the local context, with the Levenshtein spell correction outperforming the edit distance-based approach in the majority of cases. Furthermore, the study reveals that the spell correction algorithm has a greater impact on accuracy when the distance between the correct and incorrect spellings is greater.

This research uses a simplified global climate model to recreate an atmosphere similar to one proposed for an Earth-like planet at a distance from the Sun, with low temperatures and a weak water vapor cycle. By analyzing the flow patterns within this atmosphere, similarities are found between disturbances that develop and the typical storms observed on Mars, which are driven by temperature differences. The research reveals that these disturbances can lead to the formation of circulation patterns near the equator similar to those seen in the actual Martian atmosphere. The most intense patterns require more energy to develop but follow the same trend as those observed on Mars. The study's findings are consistent with earlier research on the topic and provide further evidence that baroclinic storms on Mars are not unique and can be replicated in an Earth-like atmosphere with a similar temperature profile. The results also confirm that the most intense circulation patterns are directly correlated with the presence of water vapor in the lower atmosphere. On an Earth-like planet with a weak water cycle, the most energetic patterns would be confined to the equatorial region due to the limited areas with suitable temperature conditions.

This work develops a novel method for visualizing complex representations of specific functions, utilizing a combination of Hankel paths and the coordinate plane. By integrating the Hankel path into the representation, we can effectively depict the contour that the path defines within the plane. This visualization approach enables the creation of intricate, multi-component representations that would otherwise be difficult to illustrate. As a proof of concept, we apply this methodology to depict the complex Gamma function and its reciprocal in a single coordinated image for the first time.

Quantum systems' initial non-equilibrium configurations can lead to complex dynamics, making accurate simulation of even simplest models like the linear beta-Fermi gas crucial. Building upon previous research that optimized a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing quantum correlation non-equilibrium conditions, an enhanced scheme is introduced and analyzed. This revised method accounts for non-equilibrium correlations through additional counter-term corrections in the simulation, allowing for more accurate representation of quantum fluctuations within specific energy ranges. An extended analysis on the optimal parameter selection for the linearized scheme is also provided. Using this optimized method, significant improvements in simulation accuracy for both momentum and density non-equilibrium scenarios were observed, demonstrating the scheme's capability in accurately describing quantum correlation non-equilibrium conditions.

Our proposed Knowledge Distiller, named as Focal Proxy, facilitates the development of lightweight student networks that excel compared to deep teacher networks. This distillation process occurs within a Teacher-Student framework, where the student network aims to minimize the error between its outputs and the teacher's. To achieve this, we introduce a new regularizer that focuses on the most significant errors caused by the student network. This regularizer can be viewed as a soft label, which serves as a proxy for the unknown teacher output. As a result, our method does not require the actual outputs of the deep teacher network. We conduct experiments on three datasets: MNIST, FMNIST, and WebVision, which demonstrate that our Focal Proxy Knowledge Distillation approach yields superior results compared to existing methods. On ResNet50, our method delivers comparable performance to the ground truth, with only a 10% reduction in parameters.

We introduce Bucket Elimination with Sorting (BES), an optimized algorithm for inference and optimization tasks in graphical models, building on the foundations of Bucket Elimination (BE) and Sorter. By integrating the elimination and sorting steps, BES reduces the computational complexity of these tasks. We demonstrate that BES outperforms both BE and a combination of BE and Sorter in a variety of scenarios, showing that BES is more efficient and scalable. Furthermore, we develop BES-G, an unweighted version of the algorithm suitable for applications involving unweighted graphical models.

The centralizer $Z(n)\left(\mathfrak{sl}_2\right)$ consists of linear endomorphisms that commute with a specific nilpotent linear transformation $n$. To determine the Hilbert-Poincaré series of its centralizer, we utilize a free resolution provided by the Golay-Witt theorem. This series is found to be $\frac{(2k+1)^2}{12}\cdot \mu_k(\tau)$, where $\mu_k(\tau)$ represents the number of irreducible $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-representations of highest weight $k$ and $\tau$ denotes the centralizer. Additionally, we derive an expression for the Hilbert-Poincaré series of the full centralizer $Z(n)\left(\mathfrak{sl}_2\right)$, which is discovered to be $\frac{1}{12}\sum_{k=0}^\infty (2k+1)\cdot \mu_k(\tau)$.

This study develops exact statistical testing procedures for paired-permutation models used in analysis of action-outcome relationships in cognitive experiments. A new exact algorithm is presented for the paired-permutation test, which offers a significant improvement over previously existing exact methods. In addition to the exact algorithm, a simple approximate method based on Monte Carlo sampling is also provided and found to consistently outperform the exact method. When comparing the exact and approximate methods, the new exact algorithm shows a substantial gain over previously existing exact methods. In many cases, the exact method is found to be less efficient than the approximate method. However, the exact method is necessary for using the paired-permutation models in certain situations such as data analysis.

The connection between elliptical flow $v_2$ and triangular flow $v_3$ in transverse momentum for identified particles is examined. A linear relationship with a decreasing slope is observed between the two flows for pions, strange mesons, and protons, indicating that their transverse momentum dependencies are similar but scaled by their transverse overlap ellipticity. This similarity suggests that both $v_2$ and $v_3$ are influenced by particle identification, with effects appearing in pions but disappearing in lambda baryons. Consequently, a common origin for both flows is proposed, attributed to the transverse separation between particle production regions rather than initial conditions or hydrodynamic models.

We address the challenge of identifying targets that haven't been detected and aren't currently being tracked within a network of sensors with limited fields of view. Our approach integrates a graph-based model that reflects the connections between sensors and the movement of targets through the environment. Within this model, we employ a motion prediction protocol to forecast the paths that undetected targets will take. Then, we use a consensus-based method to determine the most likely scenarios representing these targets. Our implementation utilizes a dynamic graph that updates continuously as new sensor data arrives. This allows for real-time detection of new targets and re-estimation of previously identified ones. Compared to traditional methods that rely on discrete grid representations, our graph-based approach offers significant reductions in computational complexity. In a simulated scenario with 10 sensors covering a square kilometer area, our method outperforms the others by three orders of magnitude.

The potential rewards of various actions that occur during soccer matches, such as committing a foul or the ball going out of bounds, have been found to be significantly less than the maximum possible reward of scoring a goal. This research uses a large dataset of 1500 real soccer matches to analyze these action rewards. An optimal policy that guides decision-making about taking shots on goal can be obtained using an off-the-shelf tool by 3 times in a row. The policy shows a strong preference for taking shots on goal, with the most preferred action being a shot with a 0.3 probability of success when other team's goalkeeper is far away. When the opposing team's goalkeeper is close, the policy prefers an out-of-bounds throw-in over a shot with a 0.1 probability of success. When the policy has possession of the ball in its own half, it prefers giving the ball to a teammate over taking a shot with a 0.05 probability of success. The policy also shows a dislike for taking shots on goal with a very low success probability, with the most preferred action being a foul committed by the opposing team when the policy has possession of the ball in its own half. When the policy has possession of the ball in the opposing team's half, the policy prefers an out-of-bounds throw-in over taking a shot with a 0.01 probability of success.

The widespread adoption of telework has created a pressing need for laboratory setups that can be remotely configured and monitored. In response, we present the design of an automated chemistry lab, which utilizes a robotic system to modify and analyze samples based on instructions received via the cloud. Our implementation utilizes a multi-disciplinary approach, integrating artificial intelligence, chemistry, and robotics to create a system that can accurately predict the behavior of molecular structures and automate experiments to study their properties. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our automated lab by training a machine learning model to accurately predict the fluorescence properties of biguanile compounds based on their structure, and then using that model to discover a novel, previously unknown class of compounds with desired characteristics.

We investigate the stability of solitary waves in a one-dimensional system that contains an anharmonic oscillator and is subject to the Klein-Gordon equation's dynamics. By drawing on the potential's characteristic form, we identify two distinct categories of solitary waves: regular solitary waves and oscillating solitary waves. Through a detailed analysis, we demonstrate that regular solitary waves remain stable in the presence of small anharmonic oscillator perturbations. Conversely, we find that moderate anharmonic oscillator perturbations can lead to the emergence of oscillating solitary wave patterns. Furthermore, we identify a specific threshold for anharmonic oscillator perturbations beyond which regular solitary waves become unstable and oscillating solitary waves become stable.

The paper investigates the potential discovery indicators of a neutral long-lived particle (NLVP) within the context of a hadronic collider. Since a NLVP's decay length is a critical factor in determining both its stability and search methodology, two distinct scenarios are examined: a short decay length scenario (micro-meter range) where the particle decays within the detector and a long decay length scenario (millimeter-range to meter-range) where the particle decays outside the detector. For the short decay length scenario, improvements in detection sensitivity can be achieved by enhancing the search area within the detector. In contrast, a particle with a long decay length would require the use of specific search tools such as detectors positioned outside the main detector or neutrino detectors, as well as the reconfiguration of the collider itself to identify the origin of the particle's decay site. A feasible approach to identifying a NLVP with a long decay length at a future 100 TeV collider is also proposed, involving the use of a near detector to determine the particle's presence before its decay occurs outside a main detector.

A contextualized word embedding system such as BERT uses context to determine the meaning of words with multiple definitions. Although these systems excel in identifying subtle semantic variations in language, they are not perfectly accurate when classifying changes in meaning that result from contextual modifications. To better comprehend how contextual variations impact the embeddings of words in contexts, we analyzed a dataset containing word pairs with defined semantic differences. Our findings reveal that as the contextual variety of word pairs increases, the distance between their embeddings also grows. We observed this trend even when incorporating external datasets to supplement the pre-trained model and when utilizing different contextualization techniques. Our results suggest that contextual variations directly influence the embeddings of words in contexts and that the systems' imperfections provide a unique opportunity for improvement. We developed a method called Context-Aware Embedding Refinement (CAER) that leverages information about semantic differences previously classified by the system. Our experiments showed that CAER significantly enhances the accuracy of contextualized word embeddings compared to existing strategies and yields the best outcomes when combining multiple contextually-defined embeddings.

The discovery of a new exotic nucleus with an unprecedentedly small mass value is theoretically supported by assuming the existence of ultra-light bose-einstein condensate (bec) particles within dark matter. This idea extends previous concepts as dark matter is thought to be composed of these bec-like particles rather than the typical weakly interacting massive particle model. This novel composition model requires the formation of molecular states through the interaction of these ultra-light particles which can then decay into observed nuclei. In contrast to previous studies, this research focuses on the characteristics of these molecular states and their potential detection through the observation of new isotopes. Theoretical frameworks for becoming aware of these molecular states are also discussed including the possibility of their formation within neutron stars and the potential for their detection through the decay of newly formed isotopes.

Quantum systems that are driven and oscillate between steady states offer a unique perspective when considering the possible outcomes, as these systems are not fixed in a single quantum state but rather fluctuate between multiple coherent states. By introducing an external drive that manipulates a quantum system, it is possible to create a scenario where the system constantly switches between different predefined coherent states. In a system subject to periodic driving and placed in a discrete spectrum, the possible outcomes are restricted to the pre-defined coherent states within the spectrum. To better understand these dynamics, researchers have developed an elegant framework utilizing the concept of multiple continuous-time quantum processes. By applying this framework, it is possible to examine various phenomena including the formation of entanglement between multiple systems and the creation of complex patterns of entanglement in systems with multiple parts. In particular, researchers have used this method to investigate how certain patterns of entanglement emerge when multiple systems interact with each other and are exposed to different resonant frequencies and strengths of driving forces.

We develop a quantum relational Hoare logic that enables the specification and verification of programs with multiple output relations. Building on the existing framework of QHL, our quantum relational extension includes novel relational invariants and validation rules that cater to programs processing variable-sized inputs and outputs. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, we create and verify multiple examples, including a quantum sorting algorithm that generates a stable permutation based on a given input list and its corresponding output list. Using a quantum relational Hoare proof system, we demonstrate that our algorithm generates accurate results without the need for additional post-processing. Our code is available on GitHub for reproducibility.

This study presents a novel approach for accurately determining magnetic field strengths in vector magnetic field maps by considering the fill fraction of magnetic features.  A Bayesian inference framework is utilized to classify each pixel as magnetized or non-magnetized based on local oscillatory properties derived from Helioseismics Infrared Multepurpose Imaging (HMI) data and the Magnetic Localisation Function (MLF).  The optimized threshold for the fill fraction of 20% significantly improves the accuracy of field reconstructions compared to the standard technique of using local oscillatory properties alone.  Compared to the existing method, the enhanced approach yields enhanced results with a 12.6% reduction in error and a 25.6% improvement in signal-to-noise ratio as determined by a test case involving a complex magnetic structure observed by the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) on 2017 July 15.  Furthermore, the improved technique leads to more accurate calculations of free magnetic energy with a 21.2% reduction in error.

Building upon the theory of Coxeter groups and their geometric description through their $Δ$-wedges, this research develops novel formulas counting the number of spheres and the number of spheres in a "wedge" within these structures. A generating set $\Ss$ that is minimal and connected leads to counting spheres using the roots of a polynomial whose coefficients are recursively defined based on the generators and relations of the Coxeter group. Moreover, an explicit description is provided for all possible roots of this polynomial, along with applicable examples from various Coxeter groups, including some exceptional cases of the hyperbolic groups within the $A_n\~B_i$ series and the $D_n\~B_i$ series.
This study establishes that both spherical Bertrand curves and hyperbolic Bertrand curves are necessarily straight line segments in their respective spaces.

This study examines the performance of underrepresented loss functions in machine learning, focusing on an image classification task. Contrary to conventional practice, our research investigates and compares the performance of multiple loss functions, including the KL Divergence and a normalized version of it, relative to the commonly used cross-entropy method. Our findings reveal that the underrepresented loss functions consistently yield better results, with the normalized KL Divergence emerging as the most effective option. Furthermore, we identify a direct correlation between loss function performance and the resulting model's accuracy on difficult data. To facilitate the development of loss functions, we also propose a simple regularization technique that enhances the stability of loss function optimization. Our findings suggest that loss function design plays a crucial role in determining model performance, and we make our code available on GitHub to facilitate future research.

Neural network models have excelled in predicting relations in text data, but our research reveals that these models can achieve higher accuracy when trained on a hierarchy of relation types that are categorized as follows: basic relations (e.g., cause-and-effect), general relations (e.g., part-whole), and specific relations (e.g., cause-of-disease). We conducted experiments using three different neural network models and found that supervised training on this hierarchy resulted in better performance on an available dataset compared to training on individual relation types. Notably, we observed that models trained on the hierarchy performed significantly better when identifying specific relation types but showed little improvement in cases of unclear context. To train these models, we need annotated data which we found to be scarce; therefore, we explored the option of supervised learning using automatically generated relations that are feasible given the finding that certain word combinations are associated with specific relations. Our findings suggest that neural network models can learn from a hierarchy of relation types and from generated data which leads to higher accuracy compared to traditional classification approaches and models trained on basic features.

Our proposed approach makes a significant enhancement to existing methods
that predict novel views of videos by incorporating a novel, jointly
learned set of transformation-based spatial and channel attention mechanisms
into the residual block of a convolutional neural network.  This newly
learned set of transformation-based attention mechanisms enables our method
to directly learn novel view prediction models within the same network.
Our implementation uses a combination of spatial and channel attention
mechanisms, which we have found to be highly effective.  Our method
outperforms existing research in novel view prediction by achieving the
best results in multiple benchmark tests.  Our findings suggest that
existing research methods may have limitations in novel view prediction
by showing that our simple implementation yields significantly better
results than existing research.  Our simple implementation has also been
found to be highly effective in other novel view prediction benchmarks.

Building on the concept of modifying the distance structure in graphs by truncating geodesic paths, this study delves into defining a new variant of metric dimension by setting a threshold $\tau$ and defining the truncated metric dimension as $wd_\tau(G)$, which concerns graphs where only paths of length at most $\tau$ are considered meaningful. Contrasting with the traditional definition of dimension, this variant sees significant changes as the structure of graphs with small $\tau$ is significantly altered. Specifically, graphs with $wd_\tau(G) = 1$ are referred to as "identifiable" and come with an interesting characterization. Moreover, an algorithm is provided to calculate $wd_\tau(G)$ for graphs with an acute description, and additional analysis is conducted on specific graph types, including trees, planar graphs, and cubic graphs.

This research develops an advanced signal processing technique for wearable accelerometer data, aimed at accurately identifying heart-related issues and their severity. Unlike existing methods that rely on audio data, this approach uses machine learning models to analyze raw accelerometer data. To achieve high accuracy in noisy environments, the proposed method employs a multi-step process involving feature extraction and a deep learning algorithm. This process was tested on data collected from wearables and medical equipment, demonstrating a significant enhancement in detecting cardiac abnormalities compared to existing methods. As a result, this technique offers a silent, reliable alternative for diagnosing heart conditions using wearable devices.

We discovered multiple narrow emission lines within the ultraviolet and optical spectra of three extreme starburst galaxies, identified through their extreme Balmer decrements. By analyzing these line ratios, we found all three galaxies exhibit characteristics of low-density molecular winds or have a reservoir of circumgalactic gas similar to the conditions observed in the Local Group's Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy. Notably, one of these galaxies, HCM 10, shows a significant discrepancy between its optical and UV line ratios, indicating a transition from a molecular wind regime to a higher ionization state near the starburst core.

We establish precise expressions for the velocity distribution of a second-class particle in ASEP, similar to previous work by Prolhac that focused on the discrete time evolution. Building upon the existing framework, we derive explicit formulas that account for both discrete and continuous time evolution. Moreover, we provide a detailed analysis of the limiting cases for the velocity distribution in the context of discrete time evolution.

Epidemiological studies frequently employ differential equations to model disease dynamics and analyze outbreak data. A key aspect of these studies is determining the effectiveness of contact between different population groups, which is represented by parameters in differential models. However, certain outcomes are biologically implausible, such as an infected group infecting a healthier group at a higher rate. Despite this, existing methods for inferring parameters from data do not account for these constraints. In response, we develop a framework for fitting differential models to partially observable outbreak data within the bounds of biological feasibility. Our approach utilizes a discrete search process to find the most plausible parameter values that match the data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to synthetic data sets and analyzing real-world outbreaks documented during the 1918 Spanish influenza pandemic.

By examining a combination of data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and GALEX, we identify the splitting points in U-B and NUV-r colors at approximately 10^10.5 M solar for massive early-type galaxies and 10^10.2 M solar for massive late-type galaxies. This split indicates a shift in stellar mass for both galaxy types towards hotter colors on the z=0.1 redshift slice compared to the z=0.05 slice. Additionally, we observe a slower color imbrication rate towards higher stellar masses at the center of massive late-type galaxies compared to their outskirts and a faster rate in comparison to elliptical galaxies.

Training multilingual models that can seamlessly switch between languages is highly desirable for tasks like sentiment analysis. However, creating such models is complicated and expensive, especially when there's limited available data. Our research finds that pre-trained models like the one used in our "Multilingual Sentiment Graph Learning" technique are already highly proficient and can be fine-tuned on data from a foreign language to achieve impressive results. By creating a graph that accurately maps words to their corresponding sentiments, we can significantly boost the model's classification accuracy. What's more, since there's no need to train an entirely new model, only the adjustable parts need to be fine-tuned on the foreign data, greatly reducing costs and data requirements. Our results indicate that even on unfamiliar languages like Hungarian, our method outperforms traditional methods and achieves comparable results to more sophisticated approaches that involve generating sentiment representations.

This study provides unique insights into the internal dynamics of red giant stars through the analysis of asteroseismic data from the TESS mission. A rotational profile is observed that breaks the expected logarithmic slope of 2, indicating a possible shift in rotation rate around 3 hours for KIC 9267654. Various factors are examined that could contribute to this unusual profile, including the star's chemical composition, core convection, and the presence of a binary companion. Using constraints from spectroscopic data, it is possible to rule out a significant shift in rotation rate or a binary companion as the cause. Instead, a sharp decrease in rotation rate is consistent with a layer of rapidly rotating angular momentum removed from the core through differential rotation induced by shear instability in a chemically stratified core containing 1.5 times the metallicity of the Sun. This condition is also met by another similar star, KIC 4337749, indicating that a chemically stratified core with shear instability is the most plausible explanation for these two stars.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its potential to cause harm worldwide. While various machine learning models have been developed to detect false information, they often require large amounts of labeled data, which can be difficult to obtain and maintain, especially for languages with limited resources. Our MetaFEND model addresses this issue by leveraging the strengths of both meta-learning and neural networks to effectively identify false information on Facebook with limited data. In a pilot study of 500 English articles, our model demonstrated comparable performance to a regular deep learning model. However, when the data set was expanded to include 2000 articles from a new source, our model showed a significant improvement in detection accuracy of 25.5% over the regular model.

Designs with large block sizes are crucial for advancing our understanding of complementary arrays, as they serve as optimal resolutions for dimension-reducing projections and free net constructions in optical multidimensional sensing technology. A Golay complementary array (GCA), specifically a quaternary GCA (t4-GCA), is considered the highest possible resolution for projecting free nets in two-dimensional sensing applications. However, due to the immense size requirements, there is currently a lack of proven constructions for a quaternary GCA pair (GCA2), forcing researchers to rely on recursive construction methods that are inefficient for large sizes. In contrast, binary and ternary GCAs can be easily constructed using known methods. In order to construct a quaternary GCA2 through recursive construction, appropriate pre-designed arrays of smaller sizes are necessary as input. In the case of size $n \times n$, binary GCAs are sufficient for construction purposes. However, due to the exponential growth of sizes in recursive construction methods, only a limited number of sizes that are powers of two have been successfully constructed for binary GCAs, leaving a gap in sizes that are not powers of two. In order to fill this gap, researchers have turned to partial GCAs, which still offer improved resolution over ordinary designs but require additional development due to definition complexities. In the case of ternary GCAs, pre-designed arrays of binary GCAs are necessary for construction purposes. In order to fill the gap in sizes that are not powers of two

This study develops an automated framework for defining regions of interest (ROIs) in medical images using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and demonstrates its effectiveness by applying it to a novel imaging modality, sound speed imaging (SSI), recently introduced in research on cardiac ultrasound. With minimal additional data required, our network learns to segment the ROI within CNN architectures used commonly in medical imaging, eliminating the need for precise manual definitions. We present unbiased evaluation metrics to assess the accuracy of SSI segmentation compared to traditional ultrasound images, demonstrating that our framework yields comparable results to established segmentation methods such as ITK-SNAP and shows promising potential for future research.

This paper introduces a unified framework for both supervised and unsupervised feature extraction, addressing the needs of basic and advanced machine learning techniques. Within this framework, an iterative process extracts features through a combination of data transformation and modeling, with each iteration receiving a previously determined set of features or labels. This process enables both the unsupervised extraction of initial features and the supervised refinement of those features for more complex tasks. A corresponding algorithm is presented, along with an analysis of its computational complexity. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the paper presents three different regularization techniques that can be used within this framework. One of these techniques is novel, while the others have been previously documented in the literature.

Recent advances in question-answering tasks have been achieved by models trained on structured data, specifically knowledge graphs in the form of factual triples. These models have shown promise in question-answering tasks, particularly for entities already present in the knowledge graph. Our research finds that pre-training models on knowledge graphs obtained from text data is equally effective as training models on large text corpora. This discovery suggests that knowledge graphs derived from text data can serve as a viable alternative for training models. Our findings indicate that models trained on knowledge graphs perform better in question-answering tasks for a significant majority of entities in the knowledge graph, compared to models trained on general text data. Our research indicates that the most effective way to incorporate external knowledge is to train models on knowledge graphs derived from text data. Our best model achieves the highest accuracy in question-answering tasks on a dataset of 100,000 entities, outperforming the current state of art by 20%. Our code is available for public use.

The non-linear charge distribution within a Yang-Mills field is investigated and its implications examined for both electric and magnetic fields, in the context of quantum chromodynamics (QCD). A new non-linear extension of the Hardy conjecture is proposed and proven for both field types, in a way that relates the shadow radius of black holes to their charge. Additionally, the effects of non-linear charge parameterization are examined and analyzed for both electric and magnetic fields, in relation to both the Nair-Vaidya and AdS-Schwarzschild metric combinations. A consistent framework is established that enables the connection of non-linear charge distribution patterns to observable light scattering data, in the presence of both electric and magnetic fields.

We conduct an in-depth analysis of how non-classical effects, specifically entanglement and squeezing, emerge in the context of optical tomography. Initially, we gather relevant information from the quantum state represented by a continuous-variable Gaussian state, which can be described through its first-order correlation matrix. This matrix consists of the covariance matrix and the displacement vector. Based on the Ollivier-Zeh effect, we develop a dynamics model that accounts for entanglement degradation due to environmental interactions. Subsequently, we derive conditions indicating the presence of entanglement and squeezing within the optical tomogram. Furthermore, we illustrate the applicability of these conditions through a case study involving a coupled harmonic oscillator model.

Reconstructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a complex task. However, for modules with multiplicity-free composition factors, we present a simplified approach that builds upon existing information about their submodule lattices. This method enables creating the complete lattice of submodules for any submodule of such a module, without recalursively applying standard submodules as previously suggested in literature. The approach is particularly effective when combining modules with multiplicity-free composition factors, making it ideal for use in specific scenarios like modules over a finite group whose irreducible representations are known.

We provide novel conditions for hypersurfaces to be minimal within Euclidean space, focusing on the case of hypersurfaces that are defined by a biharmonic condition. Specifically, we demonstrate that conformal recurrent biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space are minimal, and also derive a new characterization for minimal hypersurfaces without the need for the second fundamental form to be conformal recurrent.

This research provides novel definitions for p/q-regular and p/q-context-free languages over the d-dimensional integer grid ((Zp/q)d) and its subset ((Np/q)d), based on the initial study on p/q-regular and p/q-context-free languages defined for the one-dimensional integer grid ((Zp/q)). It is established that a subset of (Np/q)d is p/q-recognisable if it corresponds to a p/q-regular language over the higher-dimensional grid ((Zp/q)d), that a context-free language is p/q-context-free within the subset of (Np/q)d represented by a context-free grammar, and that a subset of (Np/q)d is p/q-context-free if it is defined by a context-free grammar over the higher-dimensional grid ((Zp/q)d). It is also demonstrated that a subset of (Np/q)d is p/q-recognisable if it is p/q-context-free, and that a context-free grammar over the higher-dimensional grid ((Zp/q)d) defines a p/q-recognisable language if it does so within the one-dimensional grid ((Zp/q)).

Theoretical frameworks such as CLN and BGL, used to study rare heavy meson decays, employ effective field theories to describe weak interaction effects. While the CLN approach uses a local operator expansion to account for decay rates, the BGL framework utilizes a 1/Nc expansion of the Wigner-Eisenhart basis to describe two-body charmless decays. Recent studies have shown that both methods yield similar results for many rare decays, although some decays fit better within one framework over the other. To further analyze these similarities and differences, researchers have developed additional two-body charmless decay patterns, including decays involving a pseudoscalar and a tensor meson, as well as decays involving two tensor mesons. Additionally, the frameworks' ability to describe three-body charmless decays was examined, focusing on decays where a pseudoscalar meson interacts with a pair of vector mesons. Overall, the research indicates that both the CLN and BGL approaches are effective tools for describing rare heavy meson decays, with both frameworks exhibiting consistent patterns in their results.

This study examines the Lyapunov exponent in dynamical systems from a
different perspective, focusing on its connection to stability through a
variational approach. Unlike traditional methods that rely heavily on
analytic computations, a straightforward way to determine the Lyapunov
exponent using existing information is derived. This derived expression can
be analyzed to discern the conditions under which the Lyapunov exponent differs
between two dynamically similar systems. Furthermore, an illustrative example
in the form of a harmonic oscillator is presented and solved, demonstrating
how the variational approach can effectively identify the formation of a
non-radiative instability ring in the phase plane by identifying the
conjunction of transversal trajectories.

This study expands upon the concept of an angle in metric spaces, building upon earlier work by Gromov and Guggenheimer, and develops tools for analyzing the shape of curves within these spaces. A novel condition is identified that differentiates between spaces capable of conformally representing their curves and those that cannot, and its direct relationship established with the existing criterion involving intrinsic curvature. Within the realm of $H$-spaces, previously undefined terms are defined: the tangent plane at a point on a curve, the curvature at a specific point on a curve, and the overall shape of a curve. Additionally, an equivalent definition is derived that focuses on the existence of limits for sequences of curves within these spaces, and the category I conformal embeddability problem is solved for all possible shapes that meet certain specifications. One notable finding is that an $H$-space with a positive curvature at a particular point on a curve within its representation cannot be conformally embedded, and an analogy is drawn with classical geometry concerning the shape of curves in Euclidean planes.

Our framework, dubbed TPC, represents a significant enhancement over the existing approaches for defending neural networks against adversarial attacks born from point cloud transformations, as it introduces a novel regularization technique that incorporates a theoretical analysis to combat adversarial creation. The analysis reveals that the optimized model parameters will compensate for network biases and maintain accuracy in the face of twisting transformations. Theoretical findings suggest that the twisted perspective is an effective tool for creating challenging data sets that outperform traditional data augmentation methods. The experimental results on multiple public data sets demonstrate that the TPC framework delivers superior defense capabilities and enhances the accuracy of models compared to alternative regularization strategies. The results also indicate that the optimized models will yield better performance when incorporating traditionally difficult twisting scenarios such as mirror-like transformations.

The development of testing frameworks and automated testing tools has provided programmers with valuable feedback on errors identified during the testing process. While these tools can direct testers to specific lines of code containing errors, an automated testing environment we call "Testbed" goes a step further by modifying the original code to fix these issues. By doing so, Testbed creates a corrected code variant that can serve as a learning example for artificial intelligence-based programming tools. Our research involves analyzing how much additional help Testbed needs to obtain with various tools, demonstrating its effectiveness with two case studies, and making the Testbed environment available for public use.

We develop a novel approach to studying G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles by connecting them with the reduction modulo p of crystalline extensions in p-adic Serre theory. Building on this connection, we demonstrate that G_K-Artin-Scheier theories encompass both classical descriptions and descriptions involving the reduction of crystalline extensions. Furthermore, we establish that these theories coincide with the p-adic Serre theory for extensions of the form F_{p^n}(\mu_{p^n}) in A_CK(p)-style and in A_CK(p^n)-style for extensions F_{p^n}(\mu_{p^n}).

This study develops and investigates the performance of a novel, self-sensing composite material system that utilizes a genetic algorithm to accurately identify damage through changes in electrical resistance. The research focuses on carbon fiber reinforced polymers (CFRP) integrated with random nanofillers to create a self-sensing capability within the material. The material's capacity to detect damage is evaluated using various phalanx impacts and Mach III testing under different conditions. The genetic algorithm is applied to a finite element model of the composite material to accurately pinpoint the location and size of damage by analyzing resistance data. The results show that the self-sensing composite material system can effectively detect damage through both laboratory testing and numerical analysis. The study finds that the system's accuracy improves with more precise resistance data, and the genetic algorithm's efficiency enhances with larger damage areas. The research provides valuable insights into the performance of the novel composite material system and its potential applications in various engineering projects.

We prove three integral identities involving the GJRR polynomial, which is a generalization of geometric vectors in higher dimensions, and the Bernoulli polynomial. The first identity we establish leads to a known integral representation of the Bernoulli polynomial. Additionally, we obtain an integral formula that results in the second derivative of the Bernoulli polynomial when integrated. Lastly, we derive an identity that yields the third derivative of the Bernoulli polynomial when integrated.

If a right-angled Artin group acting on a tree has a separating subgraph whose action results in a free product, what are the conditions under which the entire action is a free product action on the tree?

This study examines how changes in inception depth impact the convergence rate of the Nested Neumann iteration scheme for solving fixed point equations in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. A practical improvement to the existing nested Neumann algorithm is presented, which generates convergence-boosting inception depths through an iterative process. A theoretical analysis is provided to demonstrate that the optimal inception depth is directly proportional to the regularity of the underlying function. A sample function with a high order of smoothness is constructed using a nested sum of Gaussian processes, and its inception depth is found to grow polynomially with respect to its index. A specific example involving a function of order five is solved numerically to demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness.

Regrettably, our proposed contextual linear bandit algorithm that uses a context histogram, "HistLinCB," does not achieve the best results in all scenarios tested in this research. However, when the algorithm is used with a context distribution-aware policy, it delivers comparable outcomes to the benchmark. Furthermore, we observe that providing additional information about the context distribution can lead to significantly better outcomes by reducing the communication costs for linear bandits in the linear contextual bandit learning process. A theoretical analysis indicating that context distribution knowledge can significantly enhance information obtained through context selection is also presented. A practical advantage of (1 bit) binary coding as the best outcome can be achieved with the smallest amount of information (two bits are required for histogram-based approaches) when the context distribution is known and linear.

The presence of polycyclic aromatic molecules as a tracer for dust in protoplanetary disks is often assumed to indicate low temperatures in these areas. However, based on new millimeter-wave observations and the use of a 3D model that accounts for vertical dust settling, it has been found that some protoplanetary disks show enhanced cooling rates in their outer regions. These elevated rates are not consistent with the expected cooling curves, suggesting an alternative explanation. In some cases, the data indicates a critical radius where the cooling rate significantly increases, which cannot be attributed to changes in temperature or optical depth. A possible cause for this phenomenon is the formation of dust depletions in the gas phase, which would reduce the effective dust cross-section and allow more stellar radiation to reach the remaining dust particles. This theoretical framework is supported by observations of various chemical species, including formic acid, cyanamide, and diatomic carbon, which are known to be affected by dust depletion. If confirmed, this discovery would indicate that an important factor contributing to low temperatures in protoplanetary disks is not the presence of PAHs, but the presence of certain molecular species. This could have implications for understanding the formation of ice lines and planetary differentiation.

This research focuses on harmonic functions and their growth patterns in a particular geometric context. We analyze how the growth condition relates to the function's domain dimension for both analytic harmonic functions and their realizations as part of a broader analytic space. We also examine the relationship between growth conditions and the dimension of the space itself. Additionally, we investigate the connection between growth conditions and the domain dimension for all analytic harmonic functions in a specific type of geometric structure known as a gradient shrinking Ricci soliton.

Deep learning models are increasingly vulnerable to static and dynamic backdoor attacks that modify classification outcomes. While existing research on static backdoor attacks is extensive, dynamically implementing such attacks that require external information from input samples poses a significant challenge. Especially in multi-class classification tasks, creating dynamic backdoors that shift the classification outcome to a predetermined category is particularly difficult. This paper addresses this shortfall by introducing the Concept Backdoor attack, which dynamically redirects the model's classification to a specific class based on subtle changes in input features or categories. Theoretical analyses demonstrate the attack's efficacy, and practical applications confirm its effectiveness on various deep learning models and datasets.

In a learning model from distributed data, incorporating feedback from the target function is highly desirable as it enables the update process to take larger steps in a random walk. However, communicating this feedback proves challenging due to its size. A newly proposed learning algorithm, called Gradient Clip and Fuse Random Walk (GCRW), tackles this issue by initially clipping and fusion of gradient values before creating a new random walk. The algorithm's updates differ significantly from previous methods that only take small steps. Theoretical analysis reveals that GCRW achieves nearly the same learning rate as if there were no communication constraints as for an earlier developed algorithm called Optimal Random Walk (ORW). Moreover, GCRW outperforms ORW by utilizing fused gradient information, which is possible without sacrificing additional communication data. The algorithm's efficiency in practice was validated through comprehensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data sets.

This study investigates the use of interpolation-based mixing as a regularization technique in semi-supervised learning for medical image segmentation, presenting two novel methods: Consistent Mixed Regularization and Consistent Mixed Loss. A theoretical analysis is provided to demonstrate how these approaches counter label noise through the application of consistency regularization. Experiments were conducted on publicly available datasets (Hermuda and Abdomen) obtained from the Challenge on Medical Segmentation (CAMUS), comparing the proposed methods to established semi-supervised learning techniques. The results showed that the Consistent Mixed Regularization method outperformed other alternatives, achieving the highest overall accuracy of 93.1% on the Bermuda dataset.

Quantum systems exhibiting nonlocal properties such as entanglement and quantum steering aren't necessarily indistinguishable from truly correlated classical systems. Here we show that in systems where entanglement has been eliminated through particle-level entanglement reduction, truly nonlocal effects still persist and can even be measured through reduced systems' entanglement's "shadow'.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and widespread connectivity in Internet-of-Vehicles (IoV) systems has created substantial security and data privacy concerns.  As these systems generate vast amounts of data, untrusted parties may be tempted to compromise privacy in exchange for data access.  To address this issue, our proposed system employs a Blockchain-based framework that utilizes a Secret Sharing algorithm to ensure the secure storage and management of vehicle data.  By utilizing a Consortium Blockchain and a Smart Contract, data is kept private until conditions are met and verified.  To evaluate the system's effectiveness, we developed a mathematical model using the Markov Chain theory, which demonstrates the optimal number of data parts that meet specific criteria.  Our findings reveal that the system's efficiency is directly tied to the number of data parts and the number of vehicles in the network.  Our findings also indicate that the system's costs increase exponentially with the number of vehicles and data parts.  To further assess the system's viability, we conducted a simulation using real-world data from Beijing, China, which demonstrates the system's capability to handle large numbers of vehicles and data parts without significant delays.  Our proposed Blockchain-based framework provides an efficient and secure way to manage IoV data, presents several avenues for future research, including the exploration of Quantum Blockchain technologies and the development of more efficient consensus algorithms.

This research introduces the Fractional Order Hyper-Tensor product-based Long Short-Term Memory (FDHT-LSTM), an innovative neural network architecture that leverages the fractional order hyper-tensor product to efficiently implement the recurrent process in LSTMs, potentially bypassing significant memory accesses and associated power consumption. To efficiently integrate the FDHT-LSTM within regular hardware and frameworks, a comprehensive Tensor Train (TT) decomposition is proposed, enabling the implementation on conventional hardware and frameworks by fitting the fractional hyper-tensor product into a series of regular tensor products. A Markov Chain Monte Carlo method is developed to efficiently compute the fractional hyper-tensor product. Evaluations on various datasets reveal that the proposed FDHT-LSTM outperforms the traditional tensor-decomposed approach in terms of throughput and energy efficiency. Implementing the FDHT-LSTM on a NVIDIA A100 GPU shows a 2.5 times increase in throughput and a 3 times reduction in energy consumption compared to the conventional tensor-decomposed approach on the same hardware.

Recently, progress has been made toward understanding the distribution of values taken by polynomial functions over integers within a range that is bounded by a prime number. This progress involves a variant of the well-known Bateman-Horn conjecture relating to polynomial functions over the integers and was achieved through the study of how certain constant groups function within the extensions of finite characteristic and transcendental degree one. In these extensions, specific conditions apply to the polynomial functions in question. Building upon the work of K. Ono regarding the variant of the Bateman-Horn conjecture and utilizing tools from arithmetic algebraic geometry, recent findings extend the variant to include polynomials over integers that define mappings within these extensions of finite characteristic and transcendental degree one.

This research examines how a boundary within a finite domain impacts the traditional approaches used to prove blow-up occurs in solutions to the Schrödinger equation, as well as the corresponding energy and mass decay estimates. A new approach that focuses on proving a specific integral bound is necessary due to the boundary complicating the application of classical blow-up theories. Within a finite domain and with specific initial and boundary conditions, this study demonstrates that the (weighted) $L^2$ norm of solutions and their time derivatives decay over time as blow-up occurs. Consequently, this research reveals that blow-up happens in solutions within a finite domain as the energy and mass decline towards zero within the domain and vanish at the boundary.

This article examines the connections between commutative algebras of positive and zero characteristic through the lens of basic open sets in their rational prime spectrum. We establish that in the positive characteristic setting, there are no non-trivial basic open sets analogous to the sets defined by vanishing ideals of characteristic-zero algebras.

The process of selecting hypotheses based on available data is often compared and evaluated using concepts such as expected loss and risk. This research explores the idea of using utility functions, traditionally found in economics, to make informed decisions about hypothesis selection. By framing the problem in this manner, researchers can draw upon established economic theory to inform their choices. Specifically, this work examines how utility functions influence the selection of hypotheses in the context of a fixed dataset. A key discovery indicates that the structure of utility functions directly impacts the order in which hypotheses are considered, revealing an intriguing connection between utility and the concept of "nice" functions identified in the paper.

This research presents DiscSense, a multi-language semantic network datasets comprising English, French and Italian, consisting of 12000 sentences with annotated discourse markers and semantic relations. The dataset is notable for being the largest available for French and Italian, and the second-largest for English, surpassing existing datasets Weistar and SemTab. The dataset was created to address the lack of discourse marker annotated data and the limited availability of semantic relation data for certain languages. The dataset is available for public use to foster research on discourse markers and their connections to semantic relations.

We provide a comprehensive derivation demonstrating that the generalized
Jordanian twist, specifically the simple Jordanian twist, satisfies the condition
required for a $r$-twist in the context of classical rational homotopy theory.
This involves utilizing the recursive formula previously established in reference
[4]. We also include a detailed calculation illustrating how the generalized
Jordanian twist corresponds to the classical simple Jordanian twist as part of
our proof.

We provide a step-by-step construction for reversing a regular expression, addressing the containment problem in the process, and announce a symbolic decision procedure for containment in regular expressions based on Brzozowski's derivative operator and the standard definition of regular expressions.

We provide a detailed description of how conserved current block operators in CFT$_2$ shift from AdS$_3$ geodesic representation to AdS$_2$ geodesic representation within the framework of an AdS$_3$ bulk side. The conversion process involves a transformation from an AdS$_3$ geodesic operator in CFT$_2$ to an AdS$_2$ geodesic operator, which results in a change from spherical harmonics in AdS$_3$ to AdS$_2$ representation. The AdS$_2$ representation specifically takes the form of AdS$_2$ geodesic operator blocks that are conserved in CFT$_2$, which are analogous to the conserved current block operators in the AdS$_3$ representation. The conversion process also involves a shift from AdS$_3$ spherical harmonics to AdS$_2$ representation, which is particularly relevant for transforming AdS$_3$ vector harmonics in a bulk AdS$_3$ gravity model with an SL(2,$\mathbb{R}$) isometry group to AdS$_2$ representation. The converted AdS$_2$ representation is consistent with an AdS$_2$ gravity model that features an SL(2,$\mathbb{R}$) isometry group, which implies that the AdS$_2$ representation is equivalent to AdS$_3$ vector harmonics in an AdS$_3$ bulk gravity

Implementing lobster-eye optics within imaging systems offers a unique way to capture wide fields of view. A key challenge in analyzing data from such systems lies in identifying specific segments associated with different rotation angles of a cross-like image. To address this challenge, we propose an intuitive method that leverages the azimuthal rotation angle of the image. By analyzing the pattern of pixels within a specific range in a binary representation of the image, we can determine the segment of the optics system that has contributed to the image. Subsequently, we develop a straightforward way to calculate the 2D coordinates of interest within the system. Evaluating the proposed method using simulated data reveals its accuracy, and its implementation can be done efficiently on embedded systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach by applying it to real-data obtained from an actual lobster-eye optics system.

To investigate the formation of halos in the universe, a new approach has been taken by modifying the standard hydrodynamic simulation code, employing a density-only model that omits the need for the Navier-Stokes equations to evolve. Instead, the model uses the Poisson equation to directly update halo mass through the accumulation of matter within halo boundaries defined by a halo finder.
